contentBlocks.text: Yesterday you formulated a real statistical question. Today: how you actually collect data to answer it well.

Data comes in two main types: categorical (labels or categories, like favorite genre) and quantitative (numeric measurements, like books read per month). How you collect data matters just as much as what type it is. A random sample — where every member of a population has an equal chance of being chosen — produces data that genuinely represents the whole population. A convenience sample — just asking whoever's easiest to reach, like only your own friends — often introduces bias, systematically over- or under-representing certain groups. If you wanted to know how many books ALL students at a school read per month, surveying only students in the library would be a convenience sample, likely overestimating the true average. Explain why a convenience sample of 'students in the library' would bias a books-read survey specifically upward, not just randomly.
You now understand why HOW you collect data shapes whether your conclusions are trustworthy. Tomorrow we'll begin analyzing data, starting with measures of center.

objectives: Distinguish categorical data from quantitative data
Distinguish a random sample from a convenience sample and explain how the latter introduces bias
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review yesterday's statistical question.
2. Introduce categorical vs. quantitative data.
3. Introduce random vs. convenience sampling using the library example.
4. Discuss why the library sample biases specifically upward.
5. Complete the worksheet.
6. Preview tomorrow's topic: measures of center.
differentiationTips: Struggling: use a simple analogy — asking only people already at a gym about exercise habits will overestimate how much the general population exercises
Ready for more: ask them to design a genuinely random sampling method for their own Day 1 statistical question
This bias-awareness lesson is foundational — many later statistical errors trace back to a flawed sampling method, not flawed math
teacherGuide.answerKey: 1. Categorical data uses labels/categories; quantitative data uses numeric measurements. 2. A random sample gives every population member an equal chance of selection; a convenience sample only includes easily-reached individuals. 3. Surveying only library students biases the result upward specifically because students who choose to be in the library are more likely to already be readers than the general student population.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses the course's data-science inquiry cycle description (the 'collect' step), establishing sampling-bias awareness essential to trustworthy statistical conclusions.
